On rearming France, the chiefs note a plan to equip eleven or twelve French divisions. Admiral Leahy warns that de Gaulle would use such divisions as a lever for power in France itself. The Western chiefs should first agree their own strategy in Europe. They should win their leaders' approval before facing the Soviets. They should consult each other before answering any Soviet proposal. And they should hold an agreed line on Balkan or Aegean operations. On Turkey they will back the Soviet wish to force her into the war, but refuse any diversion of forces that harms approved operations. The three powers recognize Iran's contribution to the war against the common enemy. They see that the war has caused Iran special economic difficulties, and state their intent to go on providing such economic help as they can. Iran's postwar economic problems are to receive full consideration from the international conferences and agencies dealing with such matters. Stalin's messages to Roosevelt were usually brief, formal, and carefully weighed, and each one mattered out of proportion to its length. A December letter belongs to the season when the alliance was converting Tehran's promises into the campaigns of 1944. For readers, it is the Soviet voice in a record often told from Washington and London, speaking for itself.

That report claimed the fighting Poles had left Warsaw and the Germans held full control. On that basis Roosevelt said the relief problem had been solved by delay and German action, and nothing more could be done. He added that he had long been distressed by the failure to help Warsaw's defenders. He hoped Poland would still end the war among the victors.

Effective implementation of American Argentine policy, he wrote, depended on British economic cooperation, and London had so far given only tentative, highly qualified promises. Hull argued the food situation made a long contract unnecessary. Judge Byrnes had reported production in Allied areas a third above normal, with war reserves becoming surplus at peace. Beef could reach Britain from America, Canada, Australia, and other South American suppliers, including America's surplus utility beef. Books Three and Four of Locke's Essay, gathered in volume two, turn from the origin of ideas to language and to knowledge itself. Book Three asks how words hook onto ideas, and how badly they can mislead when they do not. Book Four asks what we can truly claim to know, and with what certainty.

Locke's famous distinction between primary qualities, like solidity, and secondary qualities, like color, stands here, along with his degrees of knowledge and his defense of probability where proof runs out. The volume completes empiricism's founding document. Paired with volume one, it shows a philosophy trying to be honest about the limits of the human mind.
tob-0121:
Ignatius Donnelly was a lawmaker and writer from Minnesota. His 1882 bestseller Atlantis: The Antediluvian World said the lost isle was real. It sank in one great flood, he held, and its heirs seeded all the peoples of the earth. Each flood tale in the world, for him, told of that one drowning.

He piles up rocks, myths, like words, and old authors in a bold, sure case. Scholars scoffed, but the crowds bought the book. It built the whole modern craze for Atlantis on its own. As false history it is a wild, fun read, and its mark lies on a century of lost land tales.
tob-0021:
Thecla, a young woman of Iconium, hears Paul preach and leaves her fiance and family to follow the apostle. The Acts of Paul and Thecla tells her story, and early Christians cherished it for centuries. This entry draws on a verified pre-1930 public-domain edition.

Condemned to beasts and fire, Thecla escapes again and again, and in the arena she baptizes herself in a tank of water. Some church fathers condemned the tale; many believers read it as a call to courage. Thecla became a famous saint, with shrines across the Christian East. Her story remains early Christianity's boldest tale of a woman apostle.
frus-1969-1976-chile-vol-21:
Volume twenty-one of Foreign Relations of the United States for 1969 to 1976 covers Chile from 1969 to 1973. The State Department's Office of the Historian compiled the volume from declassified records. It documents one of the darkest chapters of Cold War policy in Latin America.

The papers follow Washington's alarm at Salvador Allende's election in 1970. They record the order to make the economy scream, the Track I pressure to block Allende's confirmation, and the Track II covert action run beside it. Aid cuts, coup plotting, and contacts with Chilean officers fill the file. The record ends with the September 1973 coup that brought Pinochet to power.
woodward-homo-rhodesiensis-1921:
Arthur Smith Woodward of the British Museum announced a new fossil human in Nature in 1921. Miners at Broken Hill in Rhodesia, now Kabwe in Zambia, had found a large skull deep underground. Woodward named the species Homo rhodesiensis.

He described the skull's heavy brow, large face, and diseased teeth in detail. The find was the first archaic human fossil reported from Africa. Scholars now usually group it with Homo heidelbergensis instead. The paper still matters as the moment Africa entered the fossil human record in force. The skull remains on display and under study a century later.
sawyer-wonderfull-discoverie-edmonton-16:
Elizabeth Sawyer kept a poor home at Edmonton, north of London. The Wonderfull Discoverie of Elizabeth Sawyer, printed in 1621, tells how she came to be hanged as a witch. Her case grew out of quarrels, a curse, and a neighbor's death.

The pamphlet mixes her confession with stern moral warnings, as Stuart crime print often did. It asks readers to see God's hand and the Devil's snares in a poor woman's fall. Within the year, her story reached the stage as The Witch of Edmonton. That play kept her name alive long after the gallows.
murray-witch-cult-in-western-europe-1921:
Margaret Murray read the witch trials and saw a church where others saw a crime. The Witch-Cult in Western Europe, printed in 1921, argues the accused were heirs of an old pagan faith. Murray was a trained scholar of Egypt and of folk rite.

She holds that covens of thirteen met at sabbats to serve a horned god, age after age, under the Church's nose. Her proof is drawn from the trial records themselves, read in her own bold way. The thesis swept the field, then drew fire from later scholars. No witchcraft book of its century stirred more debate.
howard-bury-mount-everest-reconnaissance:
The first Everest reconnaissance of 1921 came home with more than maps in 1922. Mount Everest: The Reconnaissance, 1921, the official account led by Charles Howard-Bury, tells the march to the great peak. His party crossed Tibet and probed the routes to the top.

On the high snows they found tracks they could not name, and the report prints the find in plain words. Porters called the maker of the tracks a wild man of the snows. From that report grew the Abominable Snowman of world fame. The book is thus both climbing history and the start of a mystery.
geley-unconscious-conscious-1921:
Gustave Geley sought the root of strange feats in From the Unconscious to the Conscious, his book of 1921. Geley ran the chief lab for such study in Paris. He holds that man is not a fixed self, but a stream that flows from a deep hid source. That source, pressed, can push out the stuff that forms shapes in the dark room.

His scheme tries to join mind science to the seance. Death, to him, is a shift of the stream, not its end. The book is the creed back of his lab. Its bold reach still draws fans.
tischner-telepathie-hellsehen-1921:
Rudolf Tischner gave his land its first full study in Ueber Telepathie und Hellsehen, out in German in 1921. The name means on thought leaps and far sight. Tischner was a healer in Munich. He ran his own tests with cards, draws, and hid marks, then weighed the hits gainst the odds that mere chance could give the same sums.

His prose is strict, calm, and free of cult zeal. The book founds the field's line in the German tongue. Fans there cite it as their charter. Its care set a bar for all who came next.
keith-fossil-remains-java-1921:
Arthur Keith gave this round up of new fossil finds to the journal Nature in 1921. Three far flung finds fill his page: Wadjak in Java, Talgai in Australia, and Boskop in South Africa. Each had come to light in the past few years of work.

Keith sets the three frames in one world map of man's deep past. He tells what each skull shows and how it shifts the tale of the races of man. The short paper is a fine snap shot of a field in fast change at that hour.
graves-truth-about-the-protocols-1921:
Philip Graves, a Times writer in Constantinople, blew the Protocols hoax wide open in three pieces in August 1921. The Times put them in book form in London the same year. The Protocols claimed to be a secret Jewish plan to rule the world, and had spread far.

Graves sets the Protocols side by side with Joly's talk in hell of 1864. Line by line, the fake is shown to be a copy, with names swapped and the rest near word for word. His proof is the key work that named the Protocols a fake for all to see.
carbonari-memoirs-1821:
Secret groups in the south of Italy drew wide fear after revolts shook Naples in 1820. An English book of 1821, turned from a French text, gave British readers their first full report on them. Its main subject is the Carbonari, a network of lodges with oaths, grades, and signs. No author is named on the title page.

Pages describe how the Carbonari met, how new men joined, and what their rites meant. Reports of trials from 1820 show how the state struck back at the groups. The book still serves as a first-hand source on the secret groups that fought kings in Italy.
iamblichus-on-the-mysteries-taylor-1821:
Iamblichus wrote On the Mysteries in reply to a sharp foe of rite. Thomas Taylor gave the work English dress in 1821. Iamblichus was a Greek sage of the late Roman age. The book defends theurgy, the work of rites that lift the soul to the gods.

Porphyry had asked how mere rites could move high gods. Iamblichus holds that the gods gave the rites and work through them by their own will. Signs, names, and gifts all take their place in his scheme. The book is the base text for all rite magic of the West since.
flammarion-death-and-its-mystery-before-:
Camille Flammarion was a French star man with a love of the strange. His Death and Its Mystery ran to three books from 1921. Book one, Before Death, came out in the dress of E. S. Brooks. It deals with signs of the soul at work while men still live.

Dreams that come true, views at a range, and deaths felt far off fill the text. Flammarion stacks tale on tale from his vast post bag of years. He holds the count too great to brush off as chance. The set is the great store of the field in its late prime.
russell-analysis-mind-1921:
Bertrand Russell published The Analysis of Mind in 1921, a set of lectures on psychology and philosophy. Russell defends neutral monism, the view that mind and matter share one basic stuff. Sensations and images, arranged in different ways, make both minds and physical things. He draws on the behaviorism of Watson and the work of William James.

Chapters treat desire, memory, belief, and consciousness itself. Russell doubts that consciousness is a special inner light. The book became a landmark of early philosophy of mind. Its plain style suits general readers. Later philosophy of psychology still starts debates from its positions.
mctaggart-nature-existence-vol-1-1921:
J. M. E. McTaggart published The Nature of Existence, Volume 1, in 1921. McTaggart was a Cambridge philosopher known for rigorous idealist argument. This volume lays out the general features any existing thing must have. Substances, qualities, and relations are defined and tested step by step.

His famous claim that time is unreal comes in the second volume's groundwork and an earlier essay. Here he builds the system that supports such bold claims. The prose is dry, exact, and hard to skim. Philosophers of the Cambridge school debated it intensely. The work remains a peak of systematic metaphysics in English. It rewards readers who enjoy pure argument.
sapir-language-1921:
Edward Sapir was a scholar of speech who studied the Native languages of North America and taught at Ottawa and Chicago. His 1921 book Language is a plain introduction to how speech works and changes. Sapir had already spent years writing down grammars of tongues few outsiders had studied. It remains one of the most loved books in its field.

Sapir covers sound patterns, grammar, word building, and the slow drift of languages over time. He shows how speech shapes thought without trapping it, an idea later linked to his name and Benjamin Whorf's. Students still read him for his clear style and his feel for language as art.
knight-risk-uncertainty-1921:
Frank Knight was an American economist whose 1921 book Risk, Uncertainty, and Profit began as his doctoral thesis. He asks a simple question with a hard answer: why do business owners earn profit at all? Perfect competition, on paper, should grind profit down to nothing.

Knight splits risk, which can be measured and insured, from true uncertainty, which cannot be measured at all. Profit, he argues, is the pay for bearing that unmeasurable uncertainty with judgment. His split still anchors how economists think about enterprise, insurance, and the founder's role. His distinction is taught to first-year students to this day. It rewards slow reading.
say-treatise-prinsep-1821:
Jean-Baptiste Say was a French writer on trade whose Treatise on Political Economy first appeared in 1803. This English version, translated by Prinsep, was published in 1821 and carried his ideas across the Atlantic. Say wrote in the line of Adam Smith but with his own sharp twists.

The book is famous for Say's Law, the claim that making goods itself creates the means to buy them, so supply creates its own demand. Say also gives the entrepreneur, the risk-taking organizer of production, a central place in economic life. For decades his treatise served as the continent's leading guide to the subject.
keynes-treatise-probability-1921:
Before Keynes remade economics, he wrote a deep book on the logic of uncertain belief. His Treatise on Probability, published in 1921, began as a Cambridge fellowship thesis before the First World War. It treats probability as a logical relation between evidence and claim.

Keynes argues that some probabilities can be numbered, but many sound judgments rest on evidence that resists exact measure. He also weighs the strength of evidence itself, apart from the balance it strikes. The book's doubts about neat numbers quietly underlie his later economics of uncertainty. He had set the book aside when war came, then finished it in the peace.
shankara-vivekachudamani-madhavananda-19:
Shankara, the eighth-century teacher of Advaita Vedanta, wrote the Vivekachudamani, the Crest-Jewel of Discrimination, as a manual for seekers. Swami Madhavananda's 1921 translation comes from the Advaita Ashrama, the order's publishing house. The poem is the beloved handbook of its school.

In verse dialogue, Shankara teaches the student to split the real from the unreal until the self stands clear as pure awareness. Body, mind, and world are coverings; Brahman alone, he argues, is finally true. Generations of Hindu students have learned their first Vedanta from these verses, often by heart. The translation keeps the verses' direct, questioning music as far as English allows.
machen-origin-of-pauls-religion-1921:
John Gresham Machen taught New Testament at Princeton and defended orthodox Christianity against the liberal theology of his day. His Origin of Paul's Religion, published in 1921, asks where the apostle Paul's teaching came from. Machen answers with detailed scholarship rather than pulpit slogans.

He argues that Paul's religion grew from the facts of Jesus's life, death, and resurrection, not from Greek mystery cults or Jewish legend. The target is the history-of-religions school, which traced Christian ideas to pagan sources around the Mediterranean. The book won respect even from scholars who rejected Machen's conclusions.
rutherford-harp-of-god-1921:
Joseph Franklin Rutherford, the Judge who led the Bible Students after Russell's death, published The Harp of God in 1921. The book offers proof of a Creator and of his plan for mankind in catechism form. It became the Jehovah's Witnesses' first great textbook.

Questions and answers walk the student through creation, the fall, the ransom, and the coming kingdom on earth. Rutherford plays the Bible as a harp of ten strings, each string a doctrine sounding in harmony with the rest. Millions of copies went out as the movement's chief tool for teaching new believers.
shahnama-warner-vol-8-1921:
Volume 8 of the Warner Shahnama appeared in 1921, the eighth of nine volumes. Arthur and Edmond Warner had begun their English Book of Kings in 1905. Firdausi's Persian epic, which they translated, ends with the fall of the Sasanian Empire to Arab armies.

This volume brings the story near that end, through the last shahs and the invasions that broke their power. Persian tradition tells these events with grief and pride, honoring rulers who lost an empire. The translation keeps the poem's couplets in English verse where it can. Readers approaching the final volume can feel the weight of a thousand years of kings passing into memory.
galsworthy-to-let-1921:
John Galsworthy published To Let in 1921 as the closing novel of The Forsyte Saga proper. The title comes from the empty Forsyte houses standing to let after the First World War. Galsworthy set the story in 1920, with a new generation in charge.

Fleur Forsyte, Soames's daughter, falls in love with Jon, the son of Irene and Jolyon. Neither knows at first why their families hate the match. The old scandal of Soames and Irene rises again to crush the young lovers. Beneath the romance, Galsworthy records an age passing: the solid Forsyte world dissolving into a looser, sadder England.
shelley-adonais-1821:
Percy Bysshe Shelley wrote Adonais in 1821 after learning that John Keats had died in Rome at twenty-five. Shelley blamed harsh reviewers for hastening Keats's death, fairly or not. The poem appeared in Pisa that same year, in the form of a classical pastoral elegy.

Shelley mourns Adonais, his name for Keats, through shepherds, dreams, and the figures of other poets. Grief slowly turns to triumph as he argues that the dead poet's spirit joins nature and outlives his enemies. The famous lines call life a dome of many-colored glass that stains eternity. Adonais is often ranked as Shelley's greatest short poem and one of the finest elegies in English.
woolf-monday-tuesday-1921:
Virginia Woolf published Monday or Tuesday in 1921, the only book of her short fiction to appear in her lifetime. It holds just eight short pieces. Woolf and her husband Leonard printed the book themselves at their Hogarth Press, with woodcuts by her sister Vanessa Bell.

The pieces are sketches and experiments rather than plotted tales. A heron flies over a London evening, a woman's thoughts scatter through a day, and a string quartet stirs a listener's memories. Kew Gardens watches couples drift past flower beds in a haze of impressions. Woolf tests here the fluid method she would perfect in her novels. The little book is her laboratory of modernist fiction.
millay-second-april-1921:
Edna St. Vincent Millay published Second April in 1921, a year after A Few Figs from Thistles made her notorious. The title nods to Chaucer's April opening and to her own second spring as a poet. Millay was by then the best-known young poet in America.

The volume holds sonnets and lyrics of her Greenwich Village maturity: love poems, elegies, and city pieces. The famous sonnet sequence beginning Euclid alone has looked on Beauty bare stands among them. Millay's tone deepens here, trading some early sparkle for grief and reflection. Wild swans, childhood memories, and lost lovers move through the pages. Second April showed that Millay was far more than a Jazz Age sensation.
cooper-spy-1821:
James Fenimore Cooper published The Spy in 1821, his second novel and his first real success. Cooper, a New York landowner turned writer, set it in Westchester County during the Revolutionary War, a neutral ground crawling with informers. It proved American fiction could outsell British imports at home.

Harvey Birch, a humble peddler, seems to be a British spy despised by both sides. In truth he serves Washington, who watches the action disguised as a mysterious traveler. Families split between king and Congress, and loyalties stay hidden until the end. Cooper mixes battle scenes, escapes, and secret missions into a new kind of American romance. The Spy launched the historical novel in the United States.
williams-sour-grapes-1921:
Sour Grapes, published in 1921, is a book of poems by William Carlos Williams, the Rutherford doctor and poet. By this point Williams had settled into the plain, direct style that made him distinct. He writes as a man looking hard at the world right in front of him.

The poems take up flowers, fruit, weather, city streets, and passing strangers. Many are brief, built from one clear image held up to the light. Others muse on age, desire, and the limits of words themselves. Sour Grapes shows Williams in full command of his method, finding weight and music in common things.
bryant-poems-1821:
William Cullen Bryant published his first book, Poems, in 1821, when American poetry still had few names of note. Bryant had written its best-known piece, 'Thanatopsis,' while still in his teens. The slim volume gathered that poem with other early work on nature, death, and faith.

'Thanatopsis' urges readers to face death calmly, since all people return to the earth together. Other poems praise wild woods, open skies, and the quiet of country places. Bryant wrote in smooth, grave verse shaped by British models yet rooted in American scenes. The book was praised abroad and helped start a lasting American tradition of nature poetry.
chekhov-cooks-wedding-1921:
The Cook's Wedding and Other Stories appeared in English in 1921, in Constance Garnett's translation. The title story is seen through the eyes of Grisha, a boy of seven. Grisha watches the household plot to marry off the cook Pelageya to a cabman she has barely met.

The Dependents shows an old peasant begging care for his starving horse, and finding none. The Orator mocks a pompous speaker hired to praise a man he barely knew. Chekhov moves easily here between comedy and quiet sorrow. Several tales take a child's view of adult dealings, with sharp results. The volume rounds out Garnett's long Englishing of his shorter fiction.
chekhov-horse-stealers-1921:
The Horse-Stealers and Other Stories reached English in 1921 through Constance Garnett's translation. The title tale follows a hospital watchman drawn into the company of horse thieves at a lonely inn. Drink, boasting, and a rising wind build the night toward theft and flight.

The Privy Councillor draws gentle comedy from a grand official's visit to a modest country estate. Other pieces in the volume range across the steppe, the road, and the village. Chekhov knew the open southern plains from travel and wrote them with love. Wind, grass, and distance shape the moods of these tales. The volume favors his stories of travel and open country.
chekhov-schoolmaster-1921:
Garnett's Schoolmaster volume of Chekhov stories appeared in English in 1921. The title story shows a worn schoolmaster honored at a dinner after twenty-five years of service. Praise rings hollow for a man spent by routine, and he dies soon after, little noticed.

The Man in a Case gives Belikov, a teacher so afraid of life that he wraps himself in rules and galoshes. His fear poisons a whole town until his sudden death frees it. The volume also reprints The Horse-Stealers, among other tales of school, town, and country. Chekhov's portraits of small, fearful lives remain painfully fresh. Few writers have matched his mix of pity and precision.
unamuno-tragic-sense-of-life-flitch-1921:
Miguel de Unamuno published Del sentimiento trágico de la vida in Spain in 1913, and J. E. Crawford Flitch Englished it in 1921 as Tragic Sense of Life. Unamuno argues that man thinks with his whole being, not with reason alone. Reason says we die for good; the heart refuses to accept that verdict.

From that clash Unamuno builds his philosophy of faith, doubt, and hunger for eternal life. He writes as a wrestler, not a professor, and names his own unbelief honestly. The book influenced thinkers far beyond Spain in the century after. Flitch's Macmillan translation was a landmark for Unamuno in English. It remains the fullest statement of his thought.
hamsun-pan-worster-1921:
Knut Hamsun published Pan in Norway in 1894, and W. W. Worster Englished it for Knopf in 1921. Lieutenant Thomas Glahn spends a summer in a hut in Nordland, hunting and fishing with his dog Aesop. At the trading post he meets Edvarda, the merchant's daughter, and falls into a proud, halting love.

Glahn tells the tale himself, two years later, and his telling keeps slipping. Pride, jealousy, and wild joy in the northern summer drive him to strange acts. Hamsun builds the novel from Glahn's senses: light, scent, blood, and weather. Worster's translation became the classic English Pan. The book stands apart from Hunger and Growth of the Soil as his lyric peak.
menander-principal-fragments-allinson-lo:
Francis G. Allinson translated the principal fragments of Menander for the Loeb series in 1921, with the Greek text facing his English. Menander, master of Greek New Comedy, wrote over a hundred plays in Athens around 300 BCE. None survives whole; his work comes down in fragments and in lines quoted by later writers.

The fragments give sharp scenes of fathers, sons, slaves, and lovers in everyday trouble. Roman playwrights copied Menander closely, and through them his plots shaped European comedy for good. Allinson labels the book honestly as fragments, since that is all the evidence allows. Readers meet a great writer the way scholars do: in bright shards. The facing Greek keeps the original within sight.
no-plays-of-japan-waley-1921:
Arthur Waley translated sixteen Noh plays into English in The Noh Plays of Japan, published in 1921. Noh, Japan's masked theater of chant, dance, and flute, had been closed to Western readers until Waley's work. His introduction explains the stages, roles, and ghost-haunted plots that English readers were meeting for the first time.

Most Noh heroes are spirits who return to relive one binding sorrow or joy. Warriors, women, and demons appear in turn, played with stately slowness and sudden fire. Waley's plain, musical English caught the plays' strange calm. Yeats and Pound felt the influence at once in their own theater work. The volume founded the Western study of Noh.
heike-monogatari-sadler-1921:
A. L. Sadler translated the whole Heike Monogatari into English in two parts, in 1918 and 1921. The Tale of the Heike is Japan's great medieval war epic, telling the Genpei War of 1180 to 1185. The Taira clan, called the Heike, rises to glittering power, then falls to the Minamoto in five years of civil war.

Blind lute priests first spread the tale, chanting its battles and deaths across Japan. Its opening lines on the bell of impermanence set the Buddhist tone of the whole. Sadler's version, from the Transactions of the Asiatic Society of Japan, first gave English the complete epic. Pride, loyalty, and the fall of the mighty fill its pages.
nicholson-studies-in-islamic-mysticism-1:
Reynold A. Nicholson, the Cambridge scholar who translated Rumi and Hujviri, gathered his Studies in Islamic Mysticism in 1921. The essays treat the early masters of Sufism and the ideas that rule their teaching. Nicholson wrote for students who wanted the sources read with care, not the legends repeated.

He traces the growth of the doctrine that the self must pass away in God, and the lives of saints who embodied it. His method joins Arabic and Persian texts to a clear English style. The book became a foundation stone of Sufi studies in English. Readers who meet Rumi through Nicholson start here for the world that made him.
osler-evolution-modern-medicine-1921:
Osler traced the whole story of his field in The Evolution of Modern Medicine. He gave the lectures at Yale in 1913, and the book came out in 1921. From early healing and Greek medicine, he moves through the long centuries. Anatomy, surgery, and the germ theory each get their chapter in the tale.

Osler writes history as a doctor who loved old books and old doctors. His narrative gave modern medical history writing its founding shape. Readers meet the makers of medicine as working people, not statues. The Gutenberg text keeps the lectures in their spoken flow. It remains a fine first history of medicine.
veblen-engineers-price-system-1921:
Veblen turned to the technicians in The Engineers and the Price System, a short book of 1921. Engineers and production experts, he argues, know how to run industry for full output. The price system, run by owners for profit, holds them back. Sabotage of production, in his special sense, keeps prices up and goods scarce.

He sketches a soviet of engineers who might one day take charge of industry. The proposal was his most radical program, half serious and half a prod. The book states institutionalism in its boldest political form. It caught the mood of postwar unrest among technical workers. Readers still cite its contrast between making and profiting.
spr-proceedings-vol31-1921:
Parts seventy nine through eighty one and an appendix make volume thirty one, dated 1921. The SPR is now a veteran body, near forty years from its founding. Its journal keeps the founding mix of experiment, case, and criticism. Trance mediumship still supplies the longest reports.

New sittings test fresh mediums under the old safeguards. Telepathy work continues, scored with the care of long practice. Spontaneous cases arrive from a public schooled by war to ask such questions. Volume thirty one sustains the primary archive into the 1920s. Its pages show a field both older and no nearer settlement. The open file remains the society's gift.
young-journal-of-discourses-vol21:
Volume XXI of the Journal of Discourses, printed at Liverpool in 1881, carries the sermon record into the 1880s. Leading elders and apostles preach in its pages, their talks preserved just as delivered. The church they serve faces mounting pressure from the nation over its marriage practice, a theme never far away.

Doctrine and defense share the pulpit here, as speakers answer critics while teaching their own. The Journal's unedited closeness makes such moments vivid for later readers. Volume XXI holds its year in the long sequence, part of the fullest preaching archive of any American religious movement.
quimby-manuscripts-1921:
Phineas Parkhurst Quimby healed by the mind decades before his papers saw print in The Quimby Manuscripts of 1921. Horatio W. Dresser edited the writings of the Maine clockmaker turned mental healer. Quimby held that disease begins in mistaken belief, and that truth, rightly grasped, sets the body free.

His ideas seeded two movements: New Thought took them up gladly, and Christian Science grew from soil he tilled. Dresser published the manuscripts to fix Quimby's place as the source. Readers meet here the rough, earnest notes of a pioneer whose influence ran far beyond his lifetime.
chahar-maqala-browne-1921:
E. G. Browne revised his translation of the Chahar Maqala in 1921 for the Gibb Memorial series. Nizami-i-Arudi wrote the Four Discourses in the twelfth century, treating the four men a king needs near him. The secretary, the poet, the astrologer, and the physician each get a discourse, salted with tales of courts and their servants.

Anecdotes carry the teaching: how a verse saved a life, how a doctor read a pulse and a fate. Browne, the great Cambridge Persianist, loved the book's lively mix of counsel and gossip. The work remains a window on Persian court life and letters at their most humane.
basden-among-the-ibos-of-nigeria-1921:
George Thomas Basden lived thirty-five years in Nigeria and wrote Among the Ibos of Nigeria in 1921, late in that long stay. Basden, an Anglican missionary and school builder, records the Igbo world he knew at close range and loved. Chi, the personal god of each person, ancestors, dibia diviners, and the village republic of elders fill his chapters.

Markets, marriages, funerals, and the rules of a stateless, democratic people come through in practiced, concrete detail. Basden writes as a friend of his subject within a missionary's frame, and both sides of him show on the page. His ethnography remains a first source on Igbo religion and society in the early colonial years.
hutton-the-angami-nagas-1921:
John Henry Hutton worked as a colonial administrator in the Naga Hills of Assam, and he wrote about the peoples he governed. His 1921 book studies the Angami Nagas, one of the major groups of those hills, drawing on years of direct contact and local testimony.

Hutton describes village government, kinship, farming, and the great feasts of merit by which men gained honor and standing. He also covers the ancestor cult, omens, and the customs that shaped birth, marriage, and death. The book became a standard source on the Angami and a model of the administrator-ethnography of its period.
hutton-the-sema-nagas-1921:
Hutton wrote this 1921 volume as a companion to his book on the Angami Nagas, turning here to their neighbors the Sema, now often called Sumi. Like its partner, the study grew out of his years as an administrator in the Assam hills.

The account centers on the morung, the bachelors' hall where young men lived and learned tribal custom. Hutton also describes headhunting, warfare, farming, and the feasts that marked rank and wealth. Sema religion, with its spirits, omens, and rites, fills much of the book. Together the two volumes preserve a detailed picture of Naga life in the early twentieth century.
yeats-michael-robartes-1921:
Yeats published this collection in 1921, between the Irish war of independence and the civil war that followed. It is a short book with two of his most famous poems at its center.

'The Second Coming' gives the volume its power: a vision of history's center failing and a rough beast slouching toward Bethlehem. Beside it stands 'A Prayer for My Daughter', written for his infant child amid storm and political fear. Other poems honor Robert Gregory and look back at Easter 1916. The book captures a great poet watching his country and his age come apart.
lawrence-psychoanalysis-unconscious-1921:
Lawrence wrote this 1921 book as a direct attack on Freud and the psychoanalytic movement then sweeping Europe. He knew the theory well enough to respect its power, and he rejected its picture of the unconscious entirely.

For Lawrence, the unconscious is not a clinic of buried wishes but a living mystery, the source of spontaneity and growth. He argues that modern people think too much and feel too little, and that analysis makes the sickness worse. The prose is combative, funny, and deliberately unscientific. It stands as modernism's anti-Freudian manifesto, written by its most bodily thinker.
lawrence-sea-sardinia-1921:
In January 1921 Lawrence and Frieda sailed from Sicily to Sardinia for a ten-day trip, and this book is the record of it. Sea and Sardinia, published that year, is often called his finest travel writing.

Lawrence describes Cagliari, mountain villages, buses crawling through snow, and peasants whose lives seem older than history. He writes of the island as a place the modern world forgot, and he half envies it. The Mediterranean itself becomes a living presence, almost a god. Every scene is sharp with hunger, cold, color, and irritation at bad inns. Few travel books feel this awake.
conrad-notes-life-letters-1921:
Notes on Life and Letters, published in 1921, gathers Conrad's essays and occasional pieces from across his career. The sailor turned novelist writes here as a public man of letters on war, Poland, and the craft of fiction.

'The Crime of Partition' pleads Poland's cause after the First World War, and 'Poland Revisited' recalls his return to his homeland in 1914. Other pieces assess Henry James and Turgenev, masters he honored, and reflect on books and the sea. The essays show Conrad's mind at work without the mask of fiction. They remain essential reading for his admirers.
hd-hymen-1921:
Hymen, published in 1921, is a collection of poems by H. D., the pen name of Hilda Doolittle, the imagist poet Ezra Pound had launched in London. The title poem is a ritual piece for voices, built like a Greek chorus.

The poems take up marriage, myth, and the gods of Greece, retelling old stories through women's eyes. H. D.'s early imagism, with its hard, clear images, here grows more ceremonial and strange. Sea, heat, and white light run through the verse. The book shows a poet moving from imagist precision toward the mythic scale of her later epics.
moore-poems-1921:
Marianne Moore's first book, Poems, appeared in London in 1921, published by friends, H. D. and Bryher, largely without Moore's own direction. She was famously displeased, yet the slim volume fixed her standing among the modernists of two continents.

The poems show her manner already formed: precise syllabic stanzas, quotations woven into argument, and armored animals as emblems of conduct. Her subjects range from critics and poets to the pangolin-like exactitude of things well made. Moore writes with a fencer's care, every word placed. The book began one of the most exact careers in American poetry.
anderson-triumph-egg-1921:
The Triumph of the Egg, published in 1921, is Sherwood Anderson's second story collection, following Winesburg, Ohio. Its tales of small-town and farm people carry his signature figure: the grotesque, a person twisted by one truth taken too far.

The title story turns an egg-sorting father's failure into grotesque comedy. 'I Want to Know Why' gives a boy's view of racehorses and the men who handle them, and other tales follow teachers, farmers, and wanderers. Anderson writes in a plain style that gropes toward feeling. These stories helped define the modern American short story.
cardozo-nature-judicial-process-1921:
The Nature of the Judicial Process, published in 1921, prints Benjamin N. Cardozo's Storrs Lectures at Yale, the most famous lectures ever given by an American judge. Cardozo, then on New York's highest court, answers a simple question: how do judges actually decide cases?

He names four methods: logic, history, custom, and sociology, and shows judges moving among them, often without knowing which is in command. Precedent guides but does not bind absolutely; the judge legislates in the gaps. Cardozo's candor and grace made the lectures a classic of legal writing. Lawyers still assign them to every beginner.
hobhouse-rational-good-1921:
The Rational Good, published in 1921, is Hobhouse's study in the logic of practice, his fullest statement in ethics. The liberal philosopher asks what makes a good rational: not appetite, not command, but harmony realized through reason.

He defines the good as a harmony of feelings, purposes, and relations that can grow without internal war, and tests pleasure, duty, and perfection against it. Social ethics follows: a rational society is one whose order lets each part develop. The argument is systematic and humane. The book crowns the philosophical side of the New Liberalism Hobhouse had helped to build.
plos-pone-0003421:
Njideka Okubadejo and colleagues screened Parkinson's patients in Nigeria for gene faults in this 2008 study. Most cases in their group seemed sporadic, with no family pattern. Three genes were already known to raise Parkinson's risk elsewhere. The team checked those genes in the Nigerian patients.

The genes were LRRK2, PRKN, and ATXN3. Each has variants that can help trigger the disease. Data from African patients had long been thin in this field. Adding Nigerian results makes the global genetic map of Parkinson's more complete. Genetic risk clearly does not stop at the borders of Europe or North America at all.
plos-pone-0003521:
Lei Wang and co-authors described a new gene shaping rice plants in this 2008 paper. Plant shape, or architecture, limits how much rice a field can yield. The gene, named OsLIC, makes a CCCH-type zinc finger protein. Such proteins can switch other genes on and off.

OsLIC acted through brassinosteroid signaling, a plant hormone pathway. It changed leaf and tiller angles, as its name records. Breeders prize genes that tune plant shape directly. This one offers a handle for higher-yielding rice design. Leaf angle decides how much light a rice plant can catch in a dense field.
plos-pone-0003621:
Keerthi Krishnan, Nathan Salomonis, and Su Guo published this developmental biology study in PLOS ONE in 2008. It looks at Spt5, a protein that controls how genes are read in cells. The team mapped which genes Spt5 acts on as zebrafish embryos develop.

Their mapping showed Spt5 can both slow down and speed up gene reading in living embryos. Earlier lab work had hinted at this dual role, but its reach in a whole animal was unclear. Finding target genes across the embryo shows Spt5 shapes development in both directions at once.
plos-pone-0003721:
Susan Broughton, Nazif Alic, Cathy Slack, and colleagues published this aging study in PLOS ONE in 2008. The insulin signaling pathway shapes both metabolism and lifespan in many animals. Fruit flies have seven insulin-like peptides, called DILPs, each made in set tissues and stages.

The team lowered levels of one peptide, DILP2, in the flies. That change altered the flies' metabolic state while leaving the expected lifespan pattern apart from it. The split shows the other DILPs can back each other up, hiding some effects while revealing others. The work shows one pathway can split its jobs between its parts.
plos-pone-0003821:
Julien Mozziconacci, Linda Sandblad, Malte Wachsmuth, and colleagues published this biophysics study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Microtubules are the rails of the cell skeleton, built from pairs of tubulin proteins. With GTP present, purified tubulin dimers assemble into tubes in the test tube, a classic lab system.

The team found the dimers first join into small clusters, called oligomers, before joining the microtubule. That early clustering step changes the picture of how microtubules get built. It gives researchers a new stage to target when modeling or disturbing the cell skeleton.
plos-pone-0003921:
Chikara Kaito, Yosuke Omae, Yasuhiko Matsumoto, and co-authors found a gene that tames a dangerous germ in 2008. Their PLOS ONE article concerns Staphylococcus aureus, a common cause of severe infection. Colonies of this germ can spread across soft agar plates. The team compared drug-sensitive and drug-resistant strains for that spreading.

All sensitive strains spread, but most resistant strains carrying SCCmec did not. Within that region they found a gene they named fudoh. The gene curbs both colony spreading and the germ's virulence. Its presence may help explain why some resistant strains behave less aggressively.
plos-pone-0004021:
Nils T. Hagen proposed a fairer way to split authorship credit in a 2008 PLOS ONE article. Multi-author papers now dominate science publishing. Credit is often given in full to every coauthor. Or it is split equally, which inflates and flattens real contributions.

Hagen's method allocates credit harmonically by author position. First authors get the largest share, with shares falling by rank. Source-level correction aims to fix biases in citation analysis. Fairer credit would sharpen hiring and funding decisions based on records. It was printed in PLOS ONE, where the full text stays free to read.
plos-pone-0004121:
Joydeep Bhattacharya published this study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It asks whether the human brain acts more alike across its parts when a person pictures a scene than when they actually see one. The work draws on an idea from physics: near a sharp change of state, very different systems start to behave in the same shared way.

That shared behaviour is called universality, and it hints that far-apart parts of a system are linked. Bhattacharya tests whether mental imagery pushes brain activity toward that linked, universal state. The paper gives readers a physics-based way to think about how imagining and seeing may rest on the same brain workings.
plos-pone-0004221:
Anjali Nath and colleagues published this heart development study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Heart development in the womb is vital. Early embryo loss or malformation has been linked to yolk sac blood vessel defects and congenital heart defects. The molecular pathways behind these human defects remain poorly mapped.

Using proteomics, the survey of a sample's full protein set, the team found a cluster of proteins thrown off balance during cardiovascular development. That cluster points to biomarkers, measurable signs, of congenital heart defects. Catching such defects early, before or just after birth, is the long-term aim of this kind of screen.
plos-pone-0004321:
Vini Pereira, David Enard, and Adam Eyre-Walker published this evolution study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Many genomes contain large numbers of transposable elements, mobile DNA pieces, a few of which are known to regulate gene expression. Recent observations suggest these elements may have played a major role in the evolution of gene expression, since many have landed near genes.

The team measured the effect of transposable element insertions on gene expression evolution in rodents. Their analysis weighs whether the elements merely litter the genome or actively rewire it. The answer shapes how we think genomes invent new regulation.
plos-pone-0004421: In 2009, Wang, Lu, and Miao predicted microRNA company. Cepred forecast co-expression of intronic microRNAs with their host genes well. The neat tool guessed which genes travel as pairs. The method aids microRNA function research today. The predictions guide future lab work.
plos-pone-0004521: In 2009, Björklund, Ranta, and Kaitala tested evolution's true speed limit. Quantitative trait evolution under shifting environmental change was modeled. The detailed individual-based models measured adaptive capacity well. The neat study informs climate response planning. The need for answers is urgent today.
plos-pone-0004621: In 2009, Busan, Barbera, and Semenic zapped brains during reach planning. TMS effects on parietal and premotor cortex during reaching planning were timed. The magnetic pulses probed planning areas quite precisely. The study maps motor planning wiring. The activation was sequential here.
plos-pone-0004721: In 2009, Sun, Xie, and Xu mapped DNA's open stretches with a stats model. Nucleosome free regions were dissected by a segmental semi-Markov model. The open stretches emerged clearly. The method aids genomics research. The open regions matter for regulation.
dequincey-confessions-1821:
Thomas De Quincey published his Confessions in the London Magazine in September 1821, and fame came at once. He calls the piece an extract from the life of a scholar. In opening pages he explains why a sane man would bind himself to opium, the drug sold then as laudanum.

Early chapters trace the lonely youth and pain that led him to the drug for relief. Later pages turn to the grand and dreadful dreams that opium brought him at night. Part life story and part prose poetry, the book made addiction a subject for serious writing in English for the first time.
garland-daughter-middle-border-1921:
Garland's Daughter of the Middle Border won the 1922 Pulitzer Prize for biography, a note in this printing stresses. Pictures show his mother Isabel and his wife Zulime Taft, called the new daughter. Book one opens with his first winter in Chicago.

The sequel carries his life from the pioneer boy of the first volume into manhood. Marriage to Zulime Taft and years as a striving writer fill the middle chapters. A return East and a backward look at the frontier close the arc. Issued in 1921, the book crowned the career of the great chronicler of the Middle Border in fitting style.
dospassos-three-soldiers-1921:
Three Soldiers divides into six parts with blunt titles: Making the Mould, The Metal Cools, and Machines. Rust, The World Outside, and Under the Wheels close the plan. Dos Passos printed the novel in 1921, fresh from the First World War.

Part one opens with a company at attention on a parade ground at evening. Men stare ahead, tired from drilling, while cooks' smells drift on the wind. Three young Americans move from hope through disgust toward revolt and desertion. The army itself becomes the foe that crushes the human spirit, in one of the first great antiwar novels in English.
akhmatova-chetki-rosary-1921:
Anna Akhmatova published Rosary, her second book of poems, in Russian, and the 1921 printing holds the lyrics that made her famous. She wrote in clear, strict forms at a time of war and revolt. Love, loss, and a sense of doom fill these short poems.

Many lines speak in a woman's voice to a lover who is absent or untrue. Others hint at the dark years closing in on Russia. One famous line vows that she is not among those who fled. Generations of Russian readers learned these poems by heart, and they still anchor her fame.
j-p-jacobsen-mogens-and-other-stories-19:
Short tales by Jacobsen fill Mogens and Other Stories, given here in the 1921 English version. The title tale tells of young love, fresh and brief as spring. Other tales turn darker, with plague, fear, and death stalking their pages.

Jacobsen polished every sentence until it shone like a cut gem. Few writers in Danish have matched his care for sound, color, and mood. Love and plague sit side by side, beauty and dread in one hand. The book gathers the full range of his short fiction and shows why later writers held his craft in awe.
berzelius-emploi-chalumeau-1821:
Jons Jacob Berzelius teaches the blowpipe's use in chemical trials in this manual, in its 1821 French version. A flame, a tube, and a steady breath reveal what a mineral hides. Prospectors and mineralogists learned the craft from the great Swedish chemist's clear, patient pages of instruction.

Tiny beads of melted ore tell their tale by color and change. Berzelius turns a camp skill into a exact field science for travelers. His methods traveled to mines and surveys on every continent in time. The little guide helped build mineralogy as a practical art, putting a laboratory, in effect, in a coat pocket.
jesuit-relations-thwaites-vol-21:
Isaac Jogues and his captivity dominate Volume 21, published in 1898. Thwaites covers Quebec and the Hurons in the years of Jogues's ordeal. Mohawk captors seized the priest, tortured him, and held him as a slave for months.

Jogues writes of his pain with a restraint that deepens its horror. Fingers crushed, body scarred, he still seeks chances to teach and baptize. Fellow priests report his calm faith under cruel, daily abuse. Many readers rank his letters the most famous captivity account in the set. A saint's suffering, told in his own quiet and steady words, fills this volume.
journal-of-discourses-vol-21:
Volume Twenty-One, from 1881, braces for the hardest law yet. The Edmunds Act draws near, set to jail hundreds of polygamists. Votes and offices will be stripped from men who keep the doctrine.

Sermons ready the Saints for prison, fines, and public scorn ahead. Speakers call the coming storm a trial sent to sift the faithful. Old unbroken spirit answers new threats in the familiar pulpit voice. Families weigh flight, hiding, and open defiance in the talks' shadow. The volume stands on the storm's edge, and every page knows it well. Its warnings read as both prophecy and plain, practical counsel.
bailey-english-dictionary-1721:
Nathan Bailey issued his Universal Etymological English Dictionary in 1721, the most complete English word book of its day. Bailey was a schoolmaster who gathered some 40,000 entries, giving each word's origin along with its meaning. Earlier English dictionaries had been small lists of hard words; Bailey aimed at the whole language.

The entries trace words to Greek, Latin, French, and other roots, and add notes on grammar and usage. The book sold through many editions and served writers and readers for decades. Samuel Johnson borrowed heavily from it when he built his own famous dictionary a generation later. Bailey's work marks the point where English lexicography became a serious, full-scale trade.
commons-industrial-government-1921:
Commons published Industrial Government in 1921, setting out his plan for democracy inside the workplace. He had spent years in Wisconsin helping to write labor laws and run the state's industrial commission. The book distills that practice into a theory of how firms and unions should govern work together.

Commons argues that collective bargaining works like a form of self-rule for industry. Workers, through unions, gain a voice in the rules that govern their days, much as citizens gain a voice in a state. He backs the claim with studies of real firms and unions he had watched at close range. The ideas here fed directly into the labor laws of the New Deal a decade later, before that program had a name.
husserl-logische-untersuchungen-1921:
Husserl issued a second edition of his Logical Investigations in the years around 1921, revising the work that had made him famous in 1900. By then he was the master of a movement, and his own thought had moved on through the Ideas of 1913. The new edition let him bring the young breakthrough closer to the mature system.

He rewrote passages, added clarifications, and rethought parts of the sixth investigation in light of his later work. Some sections he left standing, judging them still sound. The result is phenomenology's classic in its definitive form, with the founder's second thoughts visible on the page. Comparing the two editions shows a philosopher arguing with his younger self. The volume is thus a document in the history of his thought, as well as a work of philosophy.
say-letters-to-malthus-1821:
Jean-Baptiste Say wrote his Letters to Malthus on the great question of gluts, and John Richter's English translation appeared in 1821. The two economists were friends who disagreed in public. Malthus feared that a whole economy could produce more than it could sell, leaving workers idle; Say denied the possibility.

Say argues that production itself creates the income with which goods are bought, so a general glut cannot last. Particular goods can overflow a market, he grants, but the cure is more production of what is wanted, not less of everything. Malthus answered in kind, and the friendly fight shaped the classical creed for decades. The letters are courteous, clear, and sharp at once. Economists still argue the ground these two friends staked out in 1821.
wittgenstein-logisch-philosophische-abha:
Ludwig Wittgenstein's Logisch-philosophische Abhandlung appeared in German in 1921, the journal version of the work the world knows as the Tractatus. Wittgenstein, a young Austrian who had been an artillery officer in the war, wrote most of it in the trenches and in a prison camp. He believed the book solved the problems of philosophy by drawing the border of sense.

The text is built from numbered remarks, each as compressed as a line of poetry. Its core claim: a sentence has meaning by picturing a possible state of the world, and what cannot be pictured cannot be said. Ethics, God, and the meaning of life fall on the silent side of the line. The closing words, that whereof one cannot speak, thereof one must be silent, became the most quoted sentence in modern philosophy.
cia-0000009921:
American prisoners and their detention cells, north of Chavane in Saravane province, were sighted in a January 1971 report. Saravane sits in southern Laos, astride trail routes into Vietnam's center. Seeing the cells as well as the men gave the report unusual physical detail.

Cells describe a prison better than claims do: size, bars, and guards can be checked later. Such detail helped judge whether a site was a true camp or a stopping point. It also told planners what rescue would face. This file preserves the observed cells and captives together, a ground-level view of Laotian detention.
cia-0000012321:
Helms to the Director of Central Intelligence, January 1962: the summit correspondence on the Penkovsky case continues without pause. The subject, cut short in the file, concerns military matters in the colonel's channel. Principals traded these memos back and forth even as the year's crisis deepened. Berlin's tension and Cuba's approach formed the backdrop to every page.

The files keep the dialogue at the peak intact for readers today. Case management at this level balanced a spy's safety against a nation's hunger for his product. For readers, the memo shows the operation steered from the very top, month after month.
cia-0000013121:
How the Viet Cong used American prisoners, as policy rather than chance, is studied in a CIA paper from February 1967. In the south, captives were held in jungle camps. They answered to the southern movement's own command, not to Hanoi. The paper examines the doctrine behind their treatment. Prisoners served as sources of information and as labor. Above all, they served as propaganda, exhibits in a war for world opinion.

The study shows how systematic that use was. Captivity in the south followed rules written far from the camps. For readers, the paper is the enemy's prison theory read from inside, by the side that feared it most.
cia-0000013221:
Forty-two American prisoners were held by the Viet Cong in the border country, and a CIA report from November 1966 confirms the detention. The camps sat along the South Vietnam and Cambodia border area named in the title. Forty-two captives in one report made the southern system's scale plain. It was larger, and better organized, than Washington liked to admit in public.

The report counts and places the men as sources then knew them. Each number in it was a name to someone waiting at home. For readers, the page shows the southern captivity measured whole, years before its survivors came home.
cia-0000013621:
Brazil, titled with one word, gets a CIA country brief from February 1968. The brief sketches the giant's Cold War face at a hard season. The generals ruled with full force and full pride that year. Students and workers were filling the streets against them in protest. The regime was months away from the decree that closed congress. That decree opened the dictatorship's harshest years of rule.

Such briefs caught a country at a glance for busy readers above. This one catches Brazil at the hard-liners' peak, before the iron years deepened. For readers, it is the giant in brief: vast, rich, and governed by decree.
cia-0000013921: Policy toward American prisoners and a secret hospital for their care fill a CIA report dated November 2, 1967. A hidden hospital for wounded prisoners is a striking detail. It suggests the north set apart medical care for captives, away from public view. Reports like this fed debate over how the north really treated the men it held.
cia-0000014721: USSR intelligence activities are the broad subject of a CIA file dated March 5, 1954. The title names the whole field rather than one operation. Files at this level summed up Soviet spy work as the agency saw it. Such surveys helped set the watch lists and budgets of the early Cold War security state.
cia-0000014821: Major consequences of certain U.S. courses of action on Cuba fill a CIA paper dated September 6, 1962. The paper weighed the big results that might follow American steps. Like its twin of the day before, it came just ahead of the missile crisis. The pair show estimate work at full stretch on the eve of the Cold War's sharpest hour.

Readers get a dated agency survey item, preserved under a general heading that does not name a country or a single incident.

plos-pone-0005521: Falls wreck memory loss patients, but risk factors were new going forward. Allan and team ran a forward-looking study tagging tunable fall tells in memory loss. plos-pone-0005621: Genes are controlled at a distance through DNA loops. Han and team studied how concentration and length govern DNA looping in copying. The biophysics counts long-range control. plos-pone-0005721: Red-cell hormone signal meets with blood cancer biology. Kosmider and team showed EPO down-controls Kit via Lyn kinase in blood-cancer red-cell starters. plos-pone-0006421: Smart acts need no rewards. Friston and team show free-energy sensing can teach agents tricky, bendy acts. Brains as guessers, not reward-chasers — rethinking learning, from first rules, with control theory questioned. Agents tune their senses: bendy acts, simply taught, in a bold theory paper.
plos-pone-0006521: A single-letter change erases a liver protein. Stylianou and team found an ENU-made SCARB1 mutation wipes the protein from mouse livers. The fat gate, gone — one letter, big loss, mapped, with CVD risk in view. HDL and LDL: lipid levels predict.
plos-pone-0006621: Five markers race to spot killer attacks. Carrol and team tested five germ markers in sick Malawian children. The winners save lives — kids' infection radar, tested, with early spotting. Drugs in time, death cut: CRP, PCT weighed, utility judged, severe signs.
plos-pone-0009421: Severe blood loss from trauma sets off a deadly chain reaction: the gut inflames, the lungs fail, organs shut down. In rats with trauma-induced shock, drugs that mimic estrogen's action on its receptor protected both gut and lungs from the cascade. The paper suggests an unexpected therapy for trauma patients — borrowing the hormone's protective power in the critical hours after injury.
plos-pone-0009521: The brain's sound-processing cortex is wired in vertical columns and horizontal layers — but how does information actually flow through them? Recording in cats, this study maps the functional microcircuit of the primary auditory cortex. The paper reveals the routing logic by which raw sound becomes meaningful signal.
plos-pone-0009621: Ant colonies divide labor: some forage, some patrol, some stay home. This study examines how individual ants set and break records — extreme performances — within that division. The paper finds patterns in who pushes limits, revealing how simple rules produce a colony's remarkable efficiency.
plos-pone-0010421: Clear cell kidney cancer lacks a good molecular marker. This study tests angptl4 mRNA — a hypoxia-driven gene — as a diagnostic for primary and metastatic tumors. plos-pone-0010521: The FTO gene is linked to obesity in Europeans — but does it hold across ancestries? This ARIC study finds the diabetes-obesity link differs between white and African-American participants. The paper shows genetic risk isn't one-size-fits-all.
plos-pone-0010621: ADHD persists into adulthood for many — but how much is inherited? This study estimates the heritability of ADHD traits in adults using a standard symptom index. Genes explain a substantial share. The paper puts numbers on nature's role in adult attention problems.
plos-pone-0010721: Plants sense light to shape their growth. This study builds an integrative model of phytochrome B signaling from molecules to whole plants. The paper connects light perception to physiology. The integrated model predicts how whole plants respond to shifting light cues.
plos-pone-0010821: Some pond scum can make electricity from sunlight. This study measures the light-driven current flowing from these tiny green microbes. plos-pone-0010921: Meaning feels abstract, but numbers can capture it. This study extracts principal semantic components from language to measure meaning. The paper turns semantics into data. plos-pone-0011021: Pandemic flu demands vaccines that work fast and strong. This study shows the immune booster GM-CSF raises mucosal and systemic responses to a skin-delivered H1N1 DNA vaccine in monkeys. The paper offers an adjuvant strategy. The finding aids pandemic readiness.
