frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1221:
A second Hurley dispatch to the Secretary of State bears the same date, 29 July 1945. Two cables in a day from the China post signal a file moving too fast for one report. Hurley's embassy dealt with a government, an army, and a rival party all at once.

Back-to-back dispatches let an envoy split subjects: one for the urgent, one for the standing picture. Together they kept Washington's China brief full during the summit's close. This one is the day's companion piece. Read as a pair, the two cables show the tempo of a post where the next war was already taking shape.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1321:
Parten, chief of staff of the American reparations team, wrote to Pauley, its head, on 21 July 1945. The note ran inside the mission that judged Germany's capacity to pay. Parten ran its staff work; Pauley carried its findings to the summit.

Internal notes of a mission fix facts, assign tasks, and ready the chief's brief. This one dates from the heart of the reparations fight at Potsdam. It shows the mission's machine at work behind its famous head. The figures that leaders quoted in the great rooms began in staff traffic of exactly this kind.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1421:
The Soviet delegation at Potsdam submitted a text on 14 July 1945, in the volume's closing run of conference papers. The date falls just before the conference formally opened, when delegations were tabling their opening positions.

Early texts at a summit stake out ground. A paper tabled before the leaders even sat down shows a delegation arriving with its asks already drafted. Readers can follow this Soviet text forward through the talks: which of its points the final protocol kept, and which the other powers bargained away. The closing run of the volume gathers many such texts, letting the drafting fight be read whole.
frus-1945-50-intel-d21:
General John Magruder, who now ran the Strategic Services Unit in the War Department, wrote to three intelligence chiefs at once on 1 October 1945. His unit was the surviving core of the dissolved OSS. Foreign Relations of the United States prints it in the later volume covering American intelligence between 1945 and 1950.

Magruder's letter went to the Army's intelligence chief, the Navy's, and the State Department's new research and intelligence head. That mailing list is the post-OSS world in miniature: three services and one department, each holding a piece. Readers meet here the man trying to keep the remnant alive while the pieces were argued over. His papers through the autumn form the volume's thread of survival, written from inside a unit that everyone expected to vanish.
frus-1945-50-intel-d121:
Hoover wrote to Attorney General Clark on 8 August 1946, the same day the National Intelligence Authority wrote to Clark. The FBI director's letter answers the board's move from inside the Justice Department. Foreign Relations of the United States prints it in the later volume covering American intelligence between 1945 and 1950.

Hoover rarely accepted a ruling against the bureau without putting his objection in writing to his own chief. His letter of 8 August belongs to the peak of the Latin American fight, when the board's decision on the field was being delivered. Readers can read the day whole: the authority's letter and Hoover's response, claim and counter-claim, preserved side by side. The volume's fairness in printing both is what makes it history rather than a victor's tale.
frus-1945-50-intel-d221:
Dated 18 September 1947, this memorandum runs from the Director of Central Intelligence (Hillenkoetter) to the Intelligence Advisory Board. In the printed Foreign Relations series it is document 221, in the volume on intelligence from 1945 to 1950. Congress was then debating the National Security Act, the law that would soon create the CIA and the National Security Council.

A short memo could set a meeting, kill a plan, or start one. This one played its part in that daily traffic. Kept in sequence, such memos form the true diary of the office that sent them. Alone it is a page; in sequence it is evidence of how a state taught itself a new trade.
frus-1945-50-intel-d321:
The General Counsel of the Central Intelligence Group (Houston) addressed a memorandum to the Director of Central Intelligence (Hillenkoetter) on 29 July 1947. The State Department prints it as document 321 in Foreign Relations of the United States, in the intelligence volume for 1945 to 1950. Lawmakers were close to passing the National Security Act, which would put central intelligence on a firm legal footing.

Inside the government, memos were how business got done between meetings. One put the question and the facts in front of the reader at once. A reader can watch the system think on paper: a fact here, a doubt there, a choice asked for at the end. Read next to the papers around it in the volume, it helps show how the postwar intelligence system took shape step by step.
frus-1945-50-intel-d421:
Director of Central Intelligence Roscoe Hillenkoetter wrote to the Army's assistant chief of staff for military intelligence, Bissell, on 8 May 1950. The memo is document 421 in the Foreign Relations volume on American intelligence from 1945 to 1950.

Within weeks, war in Korea would test every part of the system these men ran. In May the work was still one of charts, duties, and shared reports. The memo shows the CIA chief dealing with Army intelligence at staff level, where the real links were made. Bissell's office linked the Army's field reports to the joint picture the CIA tried to build.
frus-1861-d21:
Henry Sanford, the American minister to Belgium, wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 10 May 1861. The dispatch is document 21 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Brussels sat close to both Paris and London, and Sanford prized news from each. His reports mixed court talk with press and market word. For Washington, such letters were a cheap way to keep eyes on Europe's mood in the war's first spring. Belgium's king, Leopold, had wide family ties in Europe, which made Brussels talk worth hearing. Talk in Brussels often reached Seward before the same news came by formal note.
frus-1861-d121:
Charles Faulkner wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 15 April 1861. The dispatch is document 121 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Faulkner stayed at the Paris post until Dayton could arrive. His April report came three days after Fort Sumter, from a capital full of war talk. It shows an outgoing envoy still serving the new chief through the handover. His service bridged two parties and two cabinets in the space of a few weeks. Bridging two cabinets in weeks was a strain few envoys of the age could match.
frus-1861-d221:
By the date of 22 November 1861, Seward had new word ready for Mr. Marsh. Congress received it as Document 221 in the papers printed with the President's message that year. By then, in the autumn of the war's first year, the Lincoln government knew foreign backing could change the war's course.

The text is Washington speaking: orders, guidance, and the facts the envoy was told to stress. Alone it is a small piece of paper, but in sequence it helps show how the Union held its ground abroad. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record series, is where the full exchange can be traced.
frus-1862-d21:
By the date of 11 February 1862, Seward had new word ready for Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. Congress received it as Document 21 in the foreign affairs volume that went with the President's message. It was written in the winter of the war's second year, while the North worked to block foreign aid to the South.

The text is Washington speaking: orders, guidance, and the facts the envoy was told to stress. Letters of this kind are the raw record from which the story of wartime diplomacy is built. The Foreign Relations series, kept by the State Department's Office of the Historian, preserves the full run.
frus-1862-d121:
The mail from abroad brought Seward a letter from Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London, dated 7 August 1862. Congress received it as Document 121 in the foreign affairs volume that went with the President's message. It was written in the summer of 1862, the war's second year, while the North worked to block foreign aid to the South.

Readers get the field report side of the exchange, sent home for Seward to weigh and answer. Letters of this kind are the raw record from which the story of wartime diplomacy is built. The State Department's Office of the Historian keeps the series, called Foreign Relations of the United States.
frus-1862-d221:
On 1 July 1862 Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to William Stuart of the British legation, in a letter printed as Document 221 of the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. The letter opened the month's run of Seward-Stuart exchanges.

July began with McClellan's army pulling back from Richmond, a retreat that looked like defeat abroad. Foreign governments read Union weakness as a reason to push for a truce. Against that mood, Seward kept his tone even and his letters frequent. This one belongs to the effort to steady nerves in the first days of a bad month. Both offices kept up the formal courtesies even when their governments were near quarreling.
frus-1862-d321:
Two Dayton reports are dated 3 September 1862, and the first stands as Document 321 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. Both went from William L. Dayton in Paris to Secretary of State William H. Seward.

Dayton wrote three days after Bull Run, before the defeat's full weight had reached Paris. The French government was then drafting its proposal for a joint truce, the fall's central danger. Reports from these days show the envoy gathering the court's mood while the ground shifted under his information, a fair picture of his craft. Paris and London consulted each other often before either acted on the American war.
frus-1862-d421:
On 30 May 1862 Horace J. Perry reported from Madrid to Secretary of State William H. Seward, five days after his last letter home. The report is Document 421 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs.

Frequent short reports kept Washington current in an age when mail moved by steamer. Perry covered the Spanish court's view of the war, its Cuban concerns, and its part in the Mexican affair. In the last days of May 1862, French forces had just been checked at Puebla, news that changed the tone in Madrid. Perry's dispatches let a reader follow that shift as the legation saw it, week by week.
frus-1862-d521:
On 24 September 1862 James Shepherd Pike wrote from The Hague to Secretary of State William H. Seward. His report is Document 521 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, printed for Congress.

Pike's letter was dated two days after Lincoln issued the preliminary emancipation order, but the news had not yet reached the Netherlands. He wrote instead of the Dutch scene as it stood: cautious, commercial, and waiting on American battle news. The gap between the date on the page and the facts on the ground is the story of all these letters. Seward, reading in October, could correct for it; the modern reader should too, and will find the Hague file a clear window on that lag.
frus-1862-d621:
On 10 January 1862 Jacob S. Haldeman reported from Stockholm to Secretary of State William H. Seward. The dispatch is Document 621 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the official record for the year.

Haldeman opened the year reporting Swedish goodwill and the north's reading of the war after the Trent settlement. Sweden and Norway sent the Union settlers and sailors rather than trouble, and their government's neutrality was never in question. Still, Seward wanted every post reporting, and Stockholm's letters fixed the friendly north in his survey of Europe. The report is part of the early-1862 round of the Department's work. In that round it confirmed, capital by capital, where it stood. The crisis with Britain had by then passed.
frus-1863p1-d21:
For the last time in 1862, Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to Charles Francis Adams on 29 December. Adams was the American minister in London. The letter is document 21 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863, Seward's last to London in the old year.

Seward wrote days before the freedom edict for the enslaved took force on New Year's Day. That act would change the war's face abroad, and his envoys had to be ready to speak for it. This letter belongs to that hinge in time. It shows Washington briefing its London man at the close of a year that had tested the Union and its foreign ties alike.
frus-1863p1-d121:
Third in its set comes this letter of 16 March 1863 from Secretary of State William H. Seward to Charles Francis Adams. Adams was the American minister in London. This letter is document 121 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863.

By the third sheet, a batch turns from the great heads to the finer ones. Seward's file for Britain held many small claims and talks, each worth its own page. This letter is the third of the 16 March set. It shows the depth of the brief that one envoy carried, and the care with which Washington stocked him for it.
frus-1863p1-d221:
The mail from London dated 25 June 1863 brought Secretary of State William H. Seward this report from Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. It stands as document 221 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume. It is one of the papers the State Department later printed in its Foreign Relations series for 1863.

British yards were building two ironclad rams for the Confederacy in the summer of 1863. The fight to stop those ships reached its peak that autumn, filling the London mail. For a modern reader, it offers the war as working diplomats saw it: slow mail, sharp words, and constant risk.
frus-1863p1-d321:
A formal note dated 13 November 1862 passed from Secretary of State William H. Seward to Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington, in Washington. It stands as document 321 of the 1863 diplomatic papers. It appears in the Foreign Relations series, where the State Department printed the papers it sent with the President's yearly message to Congress.

British subjects caught up in the war, as sailors, traders, or prisoners, gave London steady grounds for protest. Seward's notes answered those complaints one case at a time. It is a small piece of a huge correspondence, but the whole picture only emerges from pieces like this one.
frus-1863p1-d421:
From the British legation in Washington on 23 March 1863, Lord Lyons sent this note to Secretary of State William H. Seward. It stands as document 421 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1863. It survives in the 1863 volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, the State Department's official record of its work abroad.

Canada bordered the Union along a long, thinly guarded line. British worries about that frontier, and American worries about plots hatched there, fed part of this mail. It dates from the spring when British debate over aiding the South was still live, and every note counted. For a modern reader, it offers the war as working diplomats saw it: slow mail, sharp words, and constant risk.
frus-1863p1-d521:
Under the date 21 May 1863, the record holds a letter from Secretary William H. Seward to Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington. America was then in the third year of its Civil War, and every letter to or from London carried weight. Such notes moved by hand between the State Department and the British legation, a few streets apart in wartime Washington.

The real subject under all the polite wording was British neutrality. Washington wanted it kept strict, and London wanted no quarrel it could avoid. British subjects caught up in the war filled many pages: men arrested, goods seized, and claims for losses that London took up with Washington. It is a small, dated piece of a very large record, and it earns its place by keeping that record complete.
frus-1863p1-d621:
Secretary William H. Seward took up his pen on 22 September 1863 and wrote to William Stuart, Britain's chargé d'affaires in Washington. The letter sits in the published record of how the Lincoln government handled foreign affairs in the autumn of 1863. With Lyons away from Washington, Stuart kept the British side of the correspondence going through the autumn of 1863.

The letter also shows the craft of the period: a few stiff phrases could carry a warning, and both sides knew how to read them. Trade ran through the whole exchange. British mills wanted Southern cotton, while Union officials watched every cargo for war goods bound to the South. That is the use of such a page: not a famous text, but a firm rung in the ladder of the record.
plos-pbio-0020021:
Xuan Wang and James E. Haber studied DNA repair in yeast for PLOS Biology in 2004. When both strands of DNA break, the cell can fix the gap by copying from a matching strand. A protein called RPA coats loose single strands of DNA during that repair.

The step in focus is strand invasion, when the broken end pushes into the intact copy to start the fix. The authors test what RPA does at that exact moment. Getting this right matters because failed repair can lead to cancer or cell death. Yeast offers a clean test bed for the basic steps. The same core repair tools work in human cells, so the lessons carry over.
plos-pbio-0020321:
Sean R. Collins, Adam Douglass, Ronald D. Vale, and their team watched prion growth in PLOS Biology in 2004. Prions are protein clumps, called amyloids, that grow as more copies of the protein join and fold the same wrong way. In yeast, this growth can be filmed and measured with care.

The team found the clumps grow by adding one protein unit at a time, not by merging smaller clumps. That single detail shapes every model of how prions spread. It rules out some theories and supports others. Amyloid growth also sits behind diseases like Alzheimer's. So a clean growth rule in yeast has reach far beyond the test tube.
plos-pbio-0020421:
Mathias Currat and Laurent Excoffier modeled ancient human mating in PLOS Biology in 2004. As modern humans spread into Europe, they met Neandertals already living there. Whether the two groups mixed has long been debated from fossils and DNA.

Their model shows that even rare mixing would likely have left clear traces in today's DNA, given how the expansion unfolded. Since such traces were then unseen, they argue the two groups did not admix, or mixed far less than some claimed. Modeling like this sets the bar for what counts as evidence. It turns a debate of impressions into a test with numbers that DNA studies can check.
plos-pone-0000121:
Rony Zachariah, Anthony David Harries, Marcel Manzi, and colleagues published this health study from rural Malawi in PLOS ONE in 2006. It concerns patients infected with both HIV and tuberculosis who were offered anti-retroviral therapy, the drugs that keep HIV in check. The team measured how many patients accepted the treatment.

Their finding, stated in the title, is blunt: acceptance was low, and the cost of transport to reach care was a key barrier. The paper shows that free medicine alone does not get people treated when a bus fare stands in the way. It remains a clear case study for programs fighting HIV in poor rural regions.
plos-pone-0000221:
Amane Koizumi, Günther Zeck, Yixin Ben, and colleagues published this methods paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. It describes organotypic culture of adult mammalian retinas, keeping the light-sensing tissue of the eye alive and working outside the body. The cultured retinas stay physiologically functional, responding much as they would in a living eye.

A working retina in a dish lets researchers test drugs and study vision diseases without whole animals at every step. The authors show their culture method preserves that function. The system is a platform for studying retinal disease and for screening treatments aimed at saving sight.
plos-pone-0000321:
Marylyn M. Addo, Rika Draenert, Almas Rathod, and colleagues published this HIV immunology paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. Fully differentiated CD8 T effector cells are the most battle-ready killer cells against HIV. The authors report these cells are detectable more often in controlled HIV-1 infection than in progressive infection, where the virus wins.

The contrast suggests that having these mature killers on hand goes with keeping the virus in check. The authors compare patients who control the virus with those who do not. The pattern helps define what a protective immune response against HIV actually looks like, a target for vaccine design.
plos-pone-0000421:
Michael P. Cusack and colleagues used network math to find the amino acids a protein can least afford to lose, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Their method needs only the protein's structure. By treating the structure as a network of contacts, they identified critical residues, the positions where change is most likely to break the protein.

Knowing the critical spots in advance guides experiments: those are the positions worth mutating, and the ones where natural variants may cause disease. A method that works from structure alone can scan proteins that have never been studied in the lab. The paper is an early example of network analysis moving into protein biology.
plos-pone-0000521:
Nils Arrigo and Claire Arnold documented escaped grapevines reshaping European landscapes, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. Many European vineyards grow on rootstocks bred in North America to resist pests; these naturalised Vitis rootstocks have spread into the wild. The team studied the consequences for the native wild grapevine.

Escaped rootstocks can hybridize with wild relatives, diluting the native gene pool, and can also carry diseases. The wild grapevine is itself a relic subspecies worth protecting. The study shows farm technology leaking into ecology. A solution bred for farms becomes a pressure on the crop's wild ancestor.
plos-pone-0000621:
Andres Baena, Alan R. Mootnick, James V. Falvo and their co-authors compared a key immune gene across primates in PLOS ONE in 2007. TNF, short for tumor necrosis factor, is a signaling protein central to the immune response. The promoter, the DNA stretch that switches the TNF gene on, is strongly conserved in mammals and especially in primates.

Small spelling differences in that promoter, called SNPs, drew the team's attention. Their title reports that these promoter patterns mark primate family relationships and trace how innate immunity evolved. Readers interested in both evolution and immunology get a case where one gene's control region tells both stories at once.
plos-pone-0000721:
Frank A. J. L. Scheer, Kenneth P. Wright, Richard E. Kronauer and colleagues tested how far the human body clock can stretch. Their 2007 PLOS ONE study was motivated by Mars: a Martian day, or sol, lasts 24.65 hours. That lies outside the range the human circadian pacemaker can entrain to under typical astronaut lighting. Failing to entrain would scramble sleep and performance.

The authors examine plasticity in the clock's intrinsic period, asking whether the period itself can adapt. If the pacemaker can lengthen its own cycle, mission planners gain a biological solution to the sol problem. The results also matter for shift workers and jet lag on Earth.
plos-pone-0000821:
Lyse A. Norian and Paul M. Allen found that anti-tumor T cells grow up fast inside tumors, but not elsewhere, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Increasing the efficacy of adoptively transferred, tumor-specific T cells is a major goal of immunotherapy, where patients receive lab-grown immune cells. A fuller grasp of the effector phase of T cell responses would clearly help. It must come from the tumor site itself. Most studies instead sample blood or lymphoid organs.

Their title reports rapid maturation of effector T cells in tumors during tumor regression, absent in lymphoid organs. The battlefield changes soldiers faster than the barracks does. Sampling tumors directly could reveal what successful immunotherapy actually looks like.
plos-pone-0000921:
Francesca Gabanella, Matthew Butchbach, Luciano Saieva and co-authors linked faulty particle assembly to severity in spinal muscular atrophy, for PLOS ONE in 2007. The disease weakens motor neurons and is caused by low levels of a protein called SMN. SMN works with partner proteins to assemble small nuclear ribonucleoproteins, machines the cell needs to process its messages.

The team asked whether how badly assembly fails matches how severe the disease is. They also found the defect hits a subset of those particles hardest. A match between a lab defect and real severity supports the idea that failed assembly drives the illness. It also points to where a therapy would need to act.
plos-pone-0001021:
Steven Frank examined the puzzle of robustness in evolution, in a solo PLOS ONE article from 2007. Organisms buffer themselves against disturbance in many ways. Repair fixes damage, feedback loops hold body systems at their set points, and chemical filters sort signal from noise.

The puzzle is that strong buffering can also permit maladaptation, hidden flaws that surface later. Frank works through why protection and fragility grow from the same machinery. The paper is theory, aimed at the logic of evolution rather than one species. Its value is a clear frame for cases from drug resistance to genetic disease, where robustness cuts both ways.
plos-pone-0001121:
Jellyfish rarely fossilize well, since their bodies are soft and mostly water. Paulyn Cartwright and co-authors report a striking exception in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. They describe jellyfish fossils preserved in unusual detail in Middle Cambrian rocks, from roughly half a billion years ago.

Cnidarians, the group that includes jellyfish, split off early in animal history, so their fossils bear on how animal life first diversified. The authors describe what these specimens preserve and what they show about early jellyfish. The finds also matter because jellyfish remain a major part of ocean plankton today.
plos-pone-0001221:
Notch signaling, a conversation between neighboring cells, decides the fates of cells throughout development. Bon-Kyoung Koo and colleagues examined a protein called Mind bomb-1 in mammalian development, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Notch signaling requires that ligand molecules on one cell be pulled inside it, a step handled by ubiquitin ligase enzymes.

The authors report an obligatory role for Mind bomb-1 in mammalian Notch signaling: without it, the pathway fails. Two families of these ligases, Neuralized and Mind bomb, were known to cooperate in flies. Showing that one is indispensable in mammals sharpens the picture of a fundamental pathway.
plos-pone-0001321:
Salvianolic acid B is one of the most active components of Salvia miltiorrhiza. That plant is a traditional Chinese herbal medicine used for disorders of the brain's blood vessels. Chen-Li Liu and colleagues studied how it protects blood vessel lining cells, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Hydrogen peroxide, an oxidant, can push endothelial cells into apoptosis, programmed cell death.

The authors report that salvianolic acid B inhibits that peroxide-induced apoptosis through regulating PI3K/Akt signaling, a major survival pathway in cells. The protective effects of the herb were known in practice, but the mechanism was not. Their work connects a traditional remedy to a defined molecular route.
plos-pone-0001421:
Sarah Chapelsky and colleagues published a 2008 PLOS ONE study on a plant compound that may block anthrax toxin. Anthrax germs owe much of their harm to a toxin that weakens host defense. A known effect is the bursting of immune cells in culture. The team tested whether the compound celastrol could stop that bursting.

In mouse immune cells, the compound did hold back toxin driven cell bursting. That marks it as a lead worth more study, not yet a drug. Leads that shield host cells take a path unlike germ killing drugs. They may keep working even when germs resist standard drugs, which keeps this line of work of interest.
plos-pone-0001521:
Clotilde Randriamampita and colleagues published a 2008 PLOS ONE study on a tool to watch T cell signals live. How a T cell tells friend from foe with such speed and care was still debated. Space and time control of signals was thought to be key. The team built a sensor that glows when a core T cell enzyme is active.

With the sensor, they watched the enzyme fire both at the contact point and at the far side of the cell. That far side firing was a surprise. Live sensors like this turn fixed cell views into films. They let labs test signal theories as the acts unfold.
plos-pone-0001621:
Anand Kolatkar, Kevin Kennedy, Dan Halabuk, and their colleagues presented a software tool called C-ME in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. C-ME stands for Collaborative Molecular Modeling Environment. It lets research teams work together in a shared 3D space in real time, even when team members are in different places.

The authors note that big projects spanning many fields now produce data stored in separate places. There is no easy way to view it as a whole. Their tool was built to close that gap for work such as proteome-wide studies, which cover all the proteins in a cell or organism. The full text explains how the tool works, what it can show, and how research and training groups can use it to study molecules together.
plos-pone-0001721:
Ziad Obermeyer, Jesse Abbott-Klafter, and Christopher J. L. Murray assessed the world's main tuberculosis strategy in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. DOTS, the WHO strategy built on directly observed treatment, had been running nearly fifteen years, yet tuberculosis stayed a major global health problem. With little hard evidence that DOTS cuts the burden, its future role was under debate.

The authors gathered empirical data on whether DOTS improved case finding or treatment success. The full text gives the countries and data sources, the measures compared, and what improvements, if any, the strategy delivered. An honest audit matters because TB programs worldwide spend heavily on this framework, and policy should follow results, not habit.
plos-pone-0001821:
Ron X. Yu and co-authors presented a method to find direct target genes of transcription factors in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. A major challenge of the post-genome era is reconstructing regulatory networks from accumulated biological knowledge. Tools for identifying direct targets, genes a factor switches on by binding them, are critical to that effort.

Their approach uses joint sequence and expression likelihood, weighing DNA sequence and activity data together. They applied it to DAF-16, a longevity-linked factor in worms. The full text gives the method and the target lists. Distinguishing direct targets from downstream echoes is what turns a gene list into a wiring diagram.
plos-pone-0001921:
Martin Alphonse and co-authors studied an allergy receptor on a white blood cell type in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. The receptor, Fc epsilon RI, binds the antibody IgE and plays a key role in allergic asthma. The team had shown that neutrophils, a front-line immune cell, from people with allergic asthma carry a working form of this receptor.

They then asked what controls how much of the receptor these cells show. Two suspects were in view: contact with allergens across the seasons, and Th-2 signals, the immune messages that drive allergy. Knowing the controls could point to new ways to calm asthma at its source.
plos-pone-0002021:
Pablo Tebas and co-authors studied what happens when HIV treatment is paused, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Cost and drug side effects once made CD4-guided pauses look attractive: stop therapy, restart when immune counts fall. The large SMART trial then reported a surprise rise in cardiovascular events after treatment interruption.

The team measured metabolic and immune activation changes during such breaks in chronic HIV infection. Their aim was to show how a pause could raise heart risk. Data of this kind ended the fashion for planned breaks and still warn any strategy that lets the virus rebound.
plos-pone-0002121:
Anna Matynia, Stephan Anagnostaras, Brian Wiltgen, and co-authors reported a mouse study in PLOS ONE in 2008 about the genes behind long-lasting memory. Early steps in forming a memory were known to need genes tied to synapses and to the making of new proteins. Far less was known about the later stages, when memories settle in for the long term.

The team ran a large reverse genetic screen, testing many genes at once to see which ones mice need for remote memory. The screen picked out two genes that play a part in that later stage. The result gives memory research new leads on how the brain keeps old memories alive.
plos-pone-0002221:
Toyoaki Natsume and co-authors studied how fission yeast pass on the special packing of their centromeres, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Centromeres are the chromosome spots where the machinery of cell division grabs hold. Their chromatin, the packing of DNA with protein, is unusual and must be copied exactly each time DNA is replicated.

The team focused on Mcl1, a helper protein for DNA polymerase alpha, the enzyme that starts new DNA strands. They found Mcl1 is required to propagate centromere structures in fission yeast. The result links the basic copying machinery to the survival of the chromosome's most vital landmark.
plos-pone-0002321:

Nur77 is a nuclear receptor that pushes young T cells to die during the selection that removes self-reactive cells. It may also act in mature T cells out in the body. Regulatory T cells, marked by Foxp3, are the immune system's peacekeepers.

The team reports that these regulatory cells resist Nur77-induced apoptosis, and that the resistance promotes the survival of transplanted organs in their models. If peacekeeper cells are built to survive death signals, boosting that trait might help transplants last without heavy drugs.

Pubertal timing starts when the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis switches back on, and both genes and environment modulate it. Inbred mouse strains differ in vaginal opening age, suggesting genetic background contributes.

A whole genome scan plus refined congenic strain analysis found a dominant X-linked region controlling that timing, per the title. Published in PLOS ONE, locating the region on the X chromosome narrows the gene hunt. The work informs study of early and delayed puberty in mammals generally. Readers can follow the full methods and data in the complete text of the article.

Marta Mastroianni, Kazuo Watanabe, Travis B. White and colleagues present this 2008 PLOS ONE work on a gene targeting tool drawn from mobile group II introns. These introns can insert themselves at exact sites in DNA by a process called retrohoming. In that process the cut-out intron RNA splices back into a DNA strand and is then copied by a protein the intron itself codes for.

The authors study how these reactions work in eukaryotes, cells with a nucleus. Readers learn the steps that let introns move and settle at chosen DNA sites. The work matters because such systems could be shaped into tools for precise gene targeting.
plos-pone-0003221:
Cristianne R. M. Frazier, Peggy Mason, Xiaoxi Zhuang and colleagues test early sugar exposure in rats in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. In modern industrial environments, that thrift may backfire.

The authors test whether sucrose exposure in early life alters adult motivation and weight gain, as the title states. Readers see development, not just adult diet, put on trial. Early feeding effects would matter for how childhood nutrition advice is framed.
plos-pone-0003321:
